comments.author: walwrangler
comments.text: The headline feature for me is incremental logical replication of DDL. We've been carrying a pile of trigger-based hacks to replicate schema changes for years, and every major upgrade I open the release notes hoping this is the one. Finally.

replies.author: tuplewrangler
replies.text: Submitter here (not a core dev, just posted it) — same. Worth noting DDL replication ships with a fairly conservative allowlist of statement types in this release; ALTER TABLE with table rewrites still isn't replicated. The docs are honest about it, which I appreciate.

replies.author: walwrangler
replies.text: Ha, of course the one I need most is the one that's excluded. Still, allowlist-and-expand is the right way to ship this. The trigger hacks live another year.

comments.author: kernelpanda
comments.text:
Buried in the release notes: the planner now uses extended statistics automatically for join selectivity estimation in more cases. I tested the beta against a warehouse workload where a 5-way join was catastrophically misplanned due to correlated columns, and it went from a nested loop disaster (11 minutes) to a hash join plan (9 seconds) with zero query changes.

That one line in the notes is going to quietly fix more production incidents than any headline feature.

replies.author: planshape
replies.text: Counterpoint from someone who's been burned: every planner improvement is also a plan-stability roulette spin. "Zero query changes" cuts both ways — some fraction of workloads out there have queries that only perform acceptably because of a mis-estimate that happened to pick a good plan. Those flip too, silently, on upgrade day.

replies.author: kernelpanda
replies.text: No argument. The mitigation is the same as always: replay your workload against the new version before flipping traffic. But yes, "the planner got smarter" is a spicy changelog line if you're running a large fleet.

replies.author: staticdrift
replies.text: This exchange is the whole database upgrade experience in miniature. Excitement, then dread, then a test plan.

comments.author: bpluscurious
comments.text: Can someone who follows development explain the async I/O changes? The notes mention direct I/O support graduating from developer-only status for data files. Does this mean the double-buffering problem (page cache + shared_buffers holding the same page twice) is finally addressed in a supported configuration?

replies.author: tuplewrangler
replies.text: Mostly yes, with caveats. Direct I/O is supported now but the guidance is that it only wins if you size shared_buffers much larger than the traditional 25% rule, since you lose the kernel page cache as a second tier. For read-heavy workloads that fit in RAM it's a real win. Mixed workloads on smaller boxes should probably leave it off. It's a tuning knob now, not a default.

comments.author: ormskeptic
comments.text: Every release thread has one of these comments so it may as well be mine: I've been running this database for fifteen years across four jobs, and the upgrade that took down production wasn't the database's fault a single time. It was always our extensions, our connection pooler config, or someone's clever query hint workaround. This project's engineering discipline is criminally underappreciated.

comments.author: lambdacurious
comments.text: The new temporal table support (PERIOD columns with system-time versioning) is the sleeper feature. Application-level audit tables are one of those things everyone builds badly — triggers that miss edge cases, history tables that drift from the source schema. Having it in the engine with FOR SYSTEM_TIME queries is a big deal for anyone in a compliance-adjacent field.

replies.author: audituar
replies.text: Agreed, though I read the fine print and versioning doesn't survive a table rewrite (e.g. ALTER COLUMN TYPE) without a documented migration dance. For an audit feature that's a meaningful footgun — the moments you change a schema are exactly the moments auditors ask about.

replies.author: lambdacurious
replies.text: Good catch, I'd missed that. Still beats hand-rolled triggers, which have the same failure mode except undocumented.

comments.author: vacuumtruck
comments.text: Small quality-of-life note: pg_upgrade now preserves optimizer statistics across major versions. If you've ever done a major upgrade and then watched your first hour of production traffic hit tables with no stats, you know. The number of people this saves from a bad Saturday is enormous.
